summary:
VoidHarvest is a web tool that helps farm managers decide which crop rotation to plant next by combining NASA Earth observations, an AI model and a few low-cost measurements on their own ground.

In Guatemala, farm managers choose rotations with little information about rain, soil moisture and heat. VoidHarvest pulls NASA data (SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, POWER weather, HLS/MODIS greenness, ECOSTRESS plant temperature and SRTM slope) and feeds it to an XGBoost model that estimates soil moisture and water stress for each zone of the farm. Because satellites only see wide areas and the soil surface, we pair them with field readings at the surface and at 30 cm. The tool compares three rotation strategies side by side and lets the manager rank them by what matters most: water, income or soil, with every number showing its source and confidence.

On 15 November 2026 our team tested the method on a farm in Jocotenango, Sacatepéquez: we measured milpa, avocado and lemon quadrants with an ESP32 and moisture and temperature sensors, timed water infiltration and interviewed the farmer.

With VoidHarvest, each season stops being a bet: managers decide with space data confirmed on their own soil.
details:
Agrarian challenges in Guatemala

Agriculture is a central source of food and work in Guatemala, yet most farms are small and decide with very little data. Many managers repeat the same crops, overuse agrochemicals such as Paraquat, and irrigate by habit rather than by need. Access to agronomists, soil labs and reliable weather information is limited, so one bad season can mean lost harvests and debt.

El Niño and climate variability

Guatemala is highly exposed to El Niño, which brings irregular rains, longer dry spells and higher temperatures, especially in the Central American Dry Corridor. These shifts make traditional planting calendars less reliable. VoidHarvest uses long-term NASA records of rainfall, soil moisture and heat to show how dry or wet a season is compared with normal, so managers can choose rotations that hold up when rains fail.

Sustainability

VoidHarvest favors rotations that protect water and soil, not only short-term income. By measuring moisture at the surface and at 30 cm and checking infiltration, it helps avoid overwatering, soil degradation and unnecessary inputs. It runs on free NASA data and sensors that cost a few dollars, so it can scale to small farms without expensive equipment.

Why Jocotenango

Jocotenango, in Sacatepéquez, is a small municipality next to Antigua Guatemala where milpa, avocado and lemon grow side by side on small plots. The farmer we interviewed told us he always rotates crops, that his soil has become drier and less fertile over the years, that he uses a herbicide costing 60 quetzales per liter, and that in the dry season he must water by hose. In the field we also observed that water drained down very quickly in this soil. These are exactly the decisions VoidHarvest aims to support, which made Jocotenango our first real test site.

What it does

VoidHarvest helps farm managers choose their next crop rotation. The manager describes the farm (crops, slope, soil and what they want to protect: water, income or soil). VoidHarvest then gathers NASA Earth observations for that location, estimates soil moisture and water stress per zone with an AI model, and compares three rotation strategies side by side, showing benefits, risks and how confident we are in each number.

How it works

- NASA data: SMAP (soil moisture), GPM IMERG (rainfall), NASA POWER (temperature, humidity, radiation, ET0), HLS/MODIS (NDVI greenness), ECOSTRESS (plant temperature) and SRTM (slope).

- AI model: an XGBoost regressor trained on these variables, with SMAP soil moisture as the target and a time-based train/test split compared against a baseline. Its output is converted into low, medium or high water stress.

- Ground truth: satellites see wide areas and only the soil surface, so we add low-cost field readings at the surface and at 30 cm to confirm or contradict the satellite estimate.

- Web app: the manager ranks rotations by priority and every number shows its source and confidence. Missing data is listed, never hidden.

Field test

On 15 November 2026 our team visited a farm in Jocotenango, Sacatepéquez, Guatemala. We measured milpa, avocado and lemon quadrants next to the roots, using an ESP32 with two resistive moisture sensors and a DS18B20 temperature probe. We timed water infiltration with a 4.9 cm PVC tube, screened pH with vinegar and baking soda, and interviewed the farmer about rotations, irrigation, soil change and costs.

Benefits and intended impact

Each season, rotation choices are a bet on rain, soil and prices. VoidHarvest makes that bet smaller with free NASA data and sensors that cost a few dollars, aimed at farm managers and agronomists working plots of 1 to 3 km². The intended impact is less wasted water, healthier soil and more stable income for farms in Guatemala and Central America.

Tools

Python, XGBoost, pandas, FastAPI, Next.js/React, TypeScript [confirm], Render (hosting), NASA Earthdata / earthaccess, NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS, ESP32 (Arduino C++), resistive soil moisture sensors, DS18B20, Cursor, GitHub.

Creativity

Instead of trusting satellites blindly, VoidHarvest puts space data and the farmer's own soil side by side and says when they disagree. It talks in plain decisions (which rotation, when to plant, where to check first) rather than raw maps.

Factors we considered

Satellite resolution (SMAP pixels cover the whole farm), the gap between surface and root-zone moisture, low budget for hardware, farmer language and trust, transparency about uncertainty, and that many challenge datasets only cover the United States, so we chose global ones.
